entries.title: Cost pass-through in the U.S. aviation industry
entries.finding: In U.S. airline data for 2000 to 2019, a 10% rise in fuel price raises legacy-carrier airfares by 0.172% and low-cost-carrier airfares by 0.351%, so the fare elasticity to fuel is small.

numbers.unit: percent change in airfare per 10 percent change in fuel price
numbers.quote: When facing a 10 % increase in fuel prices, legacy carriers’ (low-cost carriers’) airfare increases by 0.172 % (0.351 %).

entries.read_via: Publisher page fetched with the Exa fetch tool; only the highlights, abstract and title footnote were returned (the page is marked open access, but the article body was not in the fetched text).
entries.notes: Matches the lead (0.172% legacy, 0.351% low-cost). The published highlight does not say 'same quarter'; the thesis chapter the article says it is based on does, and reports the lag structure (see dong-2024-thesis-ch1). Fares are average ticket prices built from the DB1B ticket sample per the thesis; the abstract and the thesis do not mention fuel surcharges, and the thesis treats ancillary fees (bags, on-board services) as separate from the ticket fare. Conversion to a recovery share (formula only, not computed): share of the fuel cost increase recovered through revenue = (fare elasticity to the fuel price) multiplied by (passenger revenue per passenger or per seat mile) divided by (fuel cost per passenger or per seat mile), i.e. the elasticity divided by fuel cost as a share of passenger revenue, over the same horizon and holding traffic constant. The elasticity here is 0.0172 (legacy) or 0.0351 (low-cost) per 1% in the same quarter. Neither the article page nor the thesis reports fuel cost per passenger for the sample, so the share is not computed.

entries.notes: Not an empirical estimate: the bounds come from a Cournot oligopoly argument, and the abstract writes them in words ('half'), so the value 50 is a bound, not a point. Nothing is said about timing. A fuel price shock is a sector-wide cost change, so the 'more than half' bound is the relevant one for 2026; the abstract also lists exceptions (congested airports, cross-subsidisation). Conversion: the pass-through rate here is already a share of the per-unit cost change that ends up in price; to turn it into a share of the fuel bill recovered through revenue it must be multiplied by the ratio of traffic after the price rise to traffic before, which the paper does not quantify.

entries.read_via: PDF downloaded from the journal site and converted to text; quotes machine-checked against that text.
entries.notes: Timing: 'we find the effect of cost shocks on airfare to occur mainly within the same quarter'; four quarterly lags are included, and the one-quarter-lag effect is still significant but smaller. Symmetry between increases and decreases is rejected in every regression, yet the long-run level is the same for both. The author warns: 'we caution against interpreting our results as price stickiness until better data frequency is available'. The cost variable is a constructed minimum fuel cost of operating the flight (fuel price x aircraft fuel burn per nautical mile x distance), so the unit is cents of one passenger's fare per dollar of the whole flight's fuel cost. Fares are DB1B ticket fares; surcharges are not discussed. Conversion to a recovery share: multiply the cents-per-dollar figure by the number of passengers on the flight. All inputs for the paper's own illustration are in this source (150 seats, 80% occupied = 120 passengers), so, as our arithmetic on the paper's numbers: 1.6 cents x 120 = 1.92 dollars of fare revenue per dollar of fuel cost for increases in the same quarter, 1.0 cent x 120 = 1.20 for decreases, and 1.2 to 1.3 cents x 120 = 1.44 to 1.56 in the long run. The paper itself says the estimate 'can then be translated into over-shifting'. These are illustrations for one assumed aircraft, not sample-wide recovery shares.

entries.read_via: RePEc abstract page downloaded and machine-checked; the publisher page returned only the title and reference list, so the body was not read.
entries.notes: Abstract only. Design as stated there: the effect of oil price dynamics on quarterly earnings and on their predictability, where predictability is measured by 'the earnings variability based on common benchmarks and the quality of analyst forecasts issued early in the quarter'. The reference list includes Kilian (2009), which suggests the supply and demand shocks follow that decomposition, but this was not confirmed in the text. Difference from our work as far as the abstract shows: it explains how predictable earnings are across many airlines, it does not estimate a recovery share by quarter, and it does not issue or score a dated forecast for a named quarter. No coefficients are given in the abstract. The first finding (the revenue effect of demand-driven oil shocks 'dominates the cost effect of aviation fuels') is a warning that an oil price rise driven by demand looks like more than 100% recovery, so the source of the shock matters for any recovery estimate.

entries.notes: Sign reported: positive. 'The main results show a strong positive influence of fuel price fluctuation on a daily basis.' The authors explain it by market inertia and by oil price rises signalling economic growth. entries.title: Strictly Proper Scoring Rules, Prediction, and Estimation
entries.venue: Journal of the American Statistical Association 102(477)
entries.finding: A scoring rule is strictly proper when the forecaster's expected score is maximised only by reporting the true distribution, and the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) has this property for distributions with a finite first moment.
entries.read_via: Article PDF downloaded from the author's university page and converted to text; the statements below were machine-checked against that text.
entries.notes: No empirical number is taken from this paper. Exact wording checked: 'It is strictly proper if the maximum is unique.'; 'The CRPS is proper relative to the class P and strictly proper relative to the subclass P1 of the Borel probability measures that have finite first moment.'; the CRPS 'generalizes the absolute error'; it 'might serve as a standard score in evaluating probabilistic forecasts of real-valued variables'. The paper defines the CRPS in positive orientation and notes it is typically used in negative orientation, where smaller is better. In that orientation 'it generalizes the absolute error to which it reduces if F is a deterministic forecast', and 'Thus the CRPS provides a direct way to compare deterministic and probabilistic forecasts', which is what lets us score a point baseline such as the guidance midpoint against a distribution on one scale. It also proposes the interval score for prediction intervals, 'a utility function that addresses width as well as coverage'.

entries.finding: Scored with the CRPS, full distributional forecasts of quarterly earnings cut the score by 36% on average against an OLS point forecast, and the typical management forecast range has only a 30% chance of covering actual earnings.

numbers.quote: we estimate that the typical management forecast range has only a 30% chance of covering actual earnings

numbers.quote: Our test period is 2011-2021.

numbers.unit: basis points over the three-day announcement window
numbers.quote: produces hedge returns of about 60 basis points over the three-day earnings announcement window

entries.read_via: Draft PDF downloaded from a Columbia Business School seminar page and converted to text; quotes machine-checked.
entries.notes: This draft, not the current SSRN abstract, is where the CRPS is used: 'we use the CRPS as the criterion for evaluating the accuracy of our distributional forecasts', citing Gneiting and Raftery (2007). The draft describes the CRPS as extending the mean squared error to distributions, whereas Gneiting and Raftery describe it as generalising the absolute error; cite the latter for the definition. The 30% coverage figure is the closest published benchmark for how often a management guidance range contains the outcome; it is a cross-firm average, not specific to airlines. The hedge return is 60 basis points in this draft and 80 in the current SSRN abstract.

entries.authors: Bailey, D. H.; Lopez de Prado, M.
entries.title: The Deflated Sharpe Ratio: Correcting for Selection Bias, Backtest Overfitting and Non-Normality
entries.venue: Journal of Portfolio Management 40(5), 94-107 (read as the July 31, 2014 author version)
entries.finding: The Deflated Sharpe Ratio tests whether a backtested Sharpe ratio is significant after adjusting for the number of strategies tried and for non-normal returns.
entries.read_via: Author-hosted PDF downloaded and converted to text; the statements below were machine-checked. The SSRN abstract (2460551) was seen through the search tool and matches.
entries.notes: No empirical number is taken from this paper. Exact wording checked: 'DSR is a PSR where the rejection threshold is adjusted to reflect the multiplicity of trials.' and 'its expected maximum is greater than zero, even if the true SR is zero'. Inputs the method needs, as listed in the paper: the number of independent trials, the variance of the Sharpe ratios across trials, the sample length, and the skewness and kurtosis of returns. This is why every variant tried has to be recorded. The formula itself did not survive text extraction and was not transcribed.

entries.read_via: sec.gov exhibit read with the Exa fetch tool (text and the start of the statement of operations); each quoted string and the three table rows cited in the notes were confirmed by a second reader (WebFetch).
entries.notes: This is the only primary statement found of how much was actually recovered, and the only one that names the base: the year-over-year increase in fuel expense. United gives no formula and does not say which revenue is counted or what revenue it would have had without the fuel shock; a second reader asked directly whether the release defines the calculation answered no. Check on the definition, using only this release's statement of operations (three months ended June 30, USD millions): aircraft fuel 5,110 versus 2,775; total operating revenue 17,672 versus 15,236; passenger revenue 16,100 versus 13,836. Our arithmetic: fuel rose 2,335, total revenue rose 2,436 and passenger revenue rose 2,264, so raw revenue growth was about 1.04 times (total) or 0.97 times (passenger) the fuel increase. 'Approximately half' therefore cannot be the raw ratio of revenue growth to fuel growth; United must be netting out revenue it would have earned anyway (capacity growth, underlying demand), and that baseline is not disclosed. Our recovery measure needs its own stated baseline and should be compared with United's claim on that understanding. The full-year figure uses a different base ('compared to the expectation at the start of the year', at oil prices as of July 14).

entries.read_via: Transcript page downloaded and machine-checked. Marked secondary because it is a third-party transcription; the same passages were seen in four other transcripts through the search tool.
entries.notes: No definition of recovery is given on the call; a word search of the transcript for recover, recapture, pass-through and offset finds only the statements quoted here. The CEO says revenue growth is 'recovering about half the increase in fuel price' and the CFO says 'recapture 50% of the increase in fuel expense', so price and expense are used interchangeably. Two remarks cut against a clean attribution of revenue gains to fuel. Asked why prices have gone up, the CEO answered 'It’s not fuel price, and it’s not capacity' and attributed about 90% to structural cost inflation shared by all airlines. He also described the asymmetry directly: 'There was another fare increase this week as fuel started to go back up, and there were no fare decreases when fuel went down.' The CFO expects 'crack spreads to remain elevated for the remainder of the year'.

The same excerpts show the operating statistics row for average price per gallon of fuel including taxes: $4.19 versus $2.34, up 79.4%. Conversion to a recovery share (formula only): share recovered = (passenger or total revenue in the quarter minus the revenue United would have had without the fuel shock) divided by (fuel expense in the quarter minus the fuel expense it would have had without the shock). entries.venue: Investing.com article republished on Yahoo Finance Canada, March 16, 2026
entries.finding: A news report of the same UBS note says UBS assumed fuel pass-through rates of 30% to 50% across U.S. airlines and jet fuel of roughly $3 per gallon in the second half of 2026.

entries.notes: This report gives only the range across airlines, not United's 45%. The fuel assumption (about $3 in the second half) is far below the $3.69 United assumed for the third quarter in July, so the earnings estimates in this note predate the fuel prices United now guides on.
